summary: A dataset is a collection of examples organized for training, validation, or evaluation.
detail: Images, text, tables, and interaction records can all be examples. Data are commonly split into training, validation, and test sets so model selection and final evaluation use different examples.

summary: A corpus is an organized collection of language material for research, model training, or evaluation.
detail: Corpora can contain text or speech and its transcriptions. Examine sources, scale, language distribution, and filtering; a corpus is not restricted to web text.
sourceTitles: The Pile: An 800GB Dataset of Diverse Text for Language Modeling

summary: Synthetic data are generated by models, programs, or simulators.
detail: A language model can generate questions and solutions that are then filtered through rules, tests, or human review before training. Check both how much data is generated and whether it is correct.
sourceTitles: Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions

summary: Annotation adds categories, answers, bounding boxes, or other target information to raw examples.
detail: Examples include labeling reviews with positive or negative sentiment and drawing bounding boxes around pedestrians in images. Clear annotation guidelines can reduce disagreement between annotators.

summary: Data curation involves selecting, cleaning, organizing, and maintaining data to meet training goals.
detail: Curating a web dataset might involve choosing sources, removing low-quality pages and duplicates, and checking the proportions of languages and topics.
sourceTitles: The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale

summary: Data filtering retains or removes examples according to rules or model scores.
detail: For example, it can remove pages with very little body text, excessive garbled text, or repeated advertisements. Inspect examples after filtering to check that substantial amounts of desired content were not mistakenly removed.
sourceTitles: The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale

summary: Deduplication identifies and handles identical or highly similar examples.
detail: When multiple websites reproduce the same article, exact-match hashes may miss some copies. Near-duplicate detection can identify them through overlapping text fragments.
sourceTitles: Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better

summary: A data mixture specifies the proportions of different sources or tasks used during training.
detail: A mixture of 20% code and 30% encyclopedia content can describe actual sampling proportions. Repeatedly sampling a small source makes its training share larger than its share of the raw data volume.
sourceTitles: DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining

summary: Data augmentation creates training variants by transforming or combining existing examples.
detail: Some transforms preserve labels, such as suitable color changes. Detection crops require transformed boxes, while methods such as Mixup combine labels. The transformed inputs and supervision must remain consistent; preserving the original label is not mandatory.

summary: A training set contains examples used directly to fit model parameters.
detail: Training scores describe performance on examples already used for learning; they do not independently establish generalization to new examples.

summary: A validation set supports model, hyperparameter, threshold, and stopping-point selection.
detail: It does not directly fit the current model’s parameters, but it guides development decisions. After repeated selection on validation results, assess final performance on an independent test set.

summary: A test set is held-out data used to evaluate final performance after development decisions are complete.
detail: Its examples should match the target setting and independence requirements. Repeatedly choosing models or tuning against test results removes its role as an independent final evaluation.

summary: Cross-validation trains and evaluates across multiple data splits to estimate performance or select models.
detail: In k-fold validation, each fold is held out in turn. Fit preprocessing inside each training fold. Respect time or group structure; scores used for tuning are not independent final test results.

summary: Generalization is a model’s ability to apply patterns learned from training data to new examples.
detail: Specify the population, time, and environment producing those examples. Good performance on an in-distribution test set does not automatically establish reliability under distribution shifts or on new tasks.

summary: Overfitting occurs when a model learns training-sample-specific patterns that generalize poorly.
detail: Falling training loss with rising validation loss is a common sign, but a gap can also result from distribution changes or implementation errors. Check the data splits and evaluation procedure before considering better data, regularization, or early stopping. Do not repeatedly use the test set to choose when to stop.

summary: Underfitting occurs when a model has not learned the data's patterns sufficiently and performs poorly even on the training set.
detail: An overly simple model, insufficient training, or excessive regularization can cause underfitting. Examine training and validation errors together before deciding what to adjust.

summary: Regularization constrains a model or modifies training to reduce overfitting.
detail: Weight decay discourages large parameters, while dropout randomly masks some activations during training. Effects depend on the data, model, and strength; excessive regularization can underfit. Regularization does not guarantee reliability under distribution shift.

summary: Distribution shift occurs when the statistical patterns of deployment or test data differ from those of the training data.
detail: A model trained on sunny daytime road images may perform worse on rainy nighttime images. Evaluating slices by weather, region, or time can help assess the shift's effects.
sourceTitles: WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts

summary: Out-of-distribution describes inputs that differ from a specified reference distribution for training or evaluation.
detail: A truck presented to a cat-versus-dog classifier is an example from outside the expected classes; lighting or acquisition changes can also shift distributions. An unseen test image is not automatically OOD. State the reference distribution and type of shift. A confident prediction does not prove an input is in distribution.
sourceTitles: A Baseline for Detecting Misclassified and Out-of-Distribution Examples

summary: Data leakage occurs when training or model selection uses information that should be unavailable at real prediction time.
detail: Examples include fitting standardization on all data before splitting, or sharing patient records across training and test sets when evaluating new-patient performance. Whether repeated individuals cause leakage depends on the target and split unit; design evaluation around actual use.
sourceTitles: scikit-learn: Common pitfalls and data leakage

summary: Evaluation data contamination occurs when test questions, answers, or highly similar material enter a model's training data.
detail: A public question bank included in a web corpus may let the model memorize questions. Checks should consider near paraphrases, answer explanations, and data used across multiple training rounds.

summary: A baseline is a reference method or result used to assess whether a new method improves performance.
detail: It can be a simple rule, an existing open-source model, or a version without a new component. Comparisons should align data, evaluation settings, and compute budgets as closely as possible.
sourceTitles: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models

summary: A benchmark combines data, task rules, and evaluation methods for comparing model capabilities.
detail: A coding benchmark may include unit tests, a runtime environment, and time limits in addition to problems. Reproducing an evaluation requires matching these conditions.
sourceTitles: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models

summary: SOTA refers to publicly reported leading results for a specified task, dataset, and evaluation setting.
detail: A claim to "advance the state of the art" should identify the metric and comparison scope. The most accurate method may also require more inference time or a larger model.
sourceTitles: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models

summary: An ablation study removes or replaces a component to examine its role in a specified setting.
detail: For example, compare a question-answering system with and without retrieval while controlling data, model selection, and other settings. Results depend on replacements, retraining, and component interactions. A difference observed in one comparison does not establish a component’s independent contribution in every system.
sourceTitles: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models

summary: Error analysis examines failed examples and error types to identify performance bottlenecks.
detail: Question-answering errors can be divided into retrieval misses, misreading evidence, and generation errors. Counting each category helps determine which stage to improve first.

summary: Variance quantifies a random quantity’s spread through squared deviations from its mean.
detail: Variance has squared units; standard deviation is its square root. State the number of repetitions and what varied. Changing seeds captures part of training randomness, not uncertainty across test samples or populations, and a standard deviation is not a confidence interval for the mean.

summary: A random seed is a value used to initialize a pseudorandom number generator.
detail: Fixing seeds helps repeat initialization, shuffling, and sampling; control relevant libraries and devices too. Seeds alone do not guarantee bitwise agreement across versions, hardware, or nondeterministic operations. Repeating one seed does not assess variation across random runs.

summary: Reproducibility describes whether others or later runs can recreate a method and its main results from the available records.
detail: Saving data versions, dependency versions, configurations, code, and random seeds helps reproduction. Different hardware or underlying implementations can still produce numerical differences.

summary: A scaling law describes an observed relationship between model performance and parameter count, training-data volume, or computation.
detail: Researchers often fit loss curves using experiments at several scales, then estimate the benefit of a larger training budget. The relationship depends on data and training settings.
sourceTitles: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

summary: A scaling ladder runs similar configurations at progressively larger scales to observe trends and support extrapolation.
detail: For example, it can train models with 100M, 300M, and 1B parameters while recording data and compute quantities. Examine each step of the specific ladder design in the report.

summary: A metric expresses an aspect of model performance as a number that can be compared across results.
detail: Classification can use accuracy, retrieval can use recall, and code generation can use test-pass rate. Multiple metrics are usually needed to understand a system's strengths and weaknesses.

summary: Accuracy is the proportion of all predictions that are correct.
detail: If 90 of 100 images are classified correctly, accuracy is 90%. With highly imbalanced classes, also examine precision and recall for individual classes.

summary: Precision measures how many examples predicted as positive are actually positive.
detail: If a model flags 20 emails as spam and 18 really are spam, precision is 90%. It reflects the impact of false positives.

summary: Recall measures how many actual positive examples a model identifies.
detail: If there are 30 spam emails and the model finds 18, recall is 60%. Raising the threshold often reduces false positives but may also miss more positives.

summary: The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
detail: For binary classification, F1 = 2TP/(2TP + FP + FN); true negatives do not enter the calculation. Specify the positive class, threshold, and zero-denominator handling. Macro-F1 averages the F1 scores for individual classes; micro-F1 pools counts before calculating F1; weighted F1 weights each class by its number of examples. Macro-F1 is generally not the harmonic mean of macro-precision and macro-recall.

summary: ROC AUC summarizes how prediction scores rank positives relative to negatives across thresholds.
detail: The ROC curve plots true-positive against false-positive rates. Binary AUC has a positive-versus-negative ranking-probability interpretation, accounting for ties. It does not measure probability calibration or determine precision and recall at an operating threshold. Inspect those measures too, especially when positives are rare.

summary: mAP averages average precision (AP) values across classes or queries.
detail: AP is computed from the precision–recall curve or the ranks of relevant results, with conventions varying by field and evaluator. Detection mAP commonly averages classwise AP; COCO also averages over IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95. Retrieval commonly averages over queries. State matching rules, classes or queries, and thresholds before comparing.

summary: Intersection over union is the intersection area of two regions divided by their union area.
detail: IoU is 1 when predicted and ground-truth boxes overlap perfectly and 0 when they do not overlap. It is commonly used for matching in object detection and for evaluating image segmentation.

summary: MAE is the average absolute difference between predicted and true values.
detail: It has the target’s units and is zero for perfect predictions. Errors contribute linearly; state the target scale and any sample weighting.

summary: RMSE is the square root of the mean squared prediction error.
detail: It has the target’s units, while squaring makes larger errors more influential. Mean squared error (MSE) omits the square root and therefore has different units and values. Align data and scales before comparing.

summary: Perplexity is the exponential of a language model’s average negative log-probability per token.
detail: With natural logarithms, PPL = exp(mean negative log-probability). Use the same text, tokenizer, context, special tokens, and scoring rules when comparing results. Values under different tokenizations are not directly comparable. Lower perplexity means higher probability for the scored text, not automatically more accurate or factual answers.

summary: pass@k measures the probability that at least one of k generated candidates for a problem passes verification.
detail: Coding evaluations commonly use test passing as success and estimate the probability from multiple samples. Report k, sampling settings, sample count, and grader; larger k uses more attempts and compute. pass@k does not show that a system can select a correct candidate without a verifier, and passing tests does not guarantee full correctness.
sourceTitles: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
